newsitem.title: USA: U.S. factory orders post broad-based gains in January.
newsitem.headline: U.S. factory orders post broad-based gains in January.

text.p: New orders received by U.S. factories bounced back strongly in January from two months of weakness, the Commerce Department said on Thursday, posting the strongest gain in four months.

Orders were up for virtually all types of goods, rising 2.5 percent to a seasonally adjusted $323.2 billion in January following a revised decline of 1.5 percent in December and a 0.5 percent fall in November.
The January orders increase was the strongest since a 2.6 percent pickup rise in September last year. It surpassed Wall Street economists' forecasts of a 2 percent increase in January orders.
Shipments and order backlogs also rose in January, a further signal of broad-based industrial strength at the beginning of 1997.
Previously, the department said December factory orders had fallen by 1.3 percent. But it revised that to show a sharper drop.
Orders for costly durable goods like new cars and refrigerators rose in January by a revised 4 percent to $175.67 billion following a drop of 1.7 percent in December.
Orders for nondurables like food and paper products were up 0.7 percent to $147.53 billion after a 1.2 percent decrease in December.
A separate Labour Department report on Thursday also pointed to economic strength as new applications for jobless pay dropped by 6,000 to 316,000 last week.
The four-week moving average of claims, which smooths out weekly variations, was at its lowest in close to eight years, indicating strong rates of job creation.
The January factory orders report showed orders for transportation equipment grew by 2.5 percent to $42.69 billion after a 0.6 percent decline in December.
Transportation is the largest single category of factory orders.
Shipments of motor vehicles and parts increased 8.6 percent in January to $28.38 billion after a 3.8 percent fall in December. In the automobile industry, shipments correspond to orders.

Excluding transportation, factory orders were up 2.5 percent in January after dropping 1.6 percent in December. The department said it was the largest monthly gain in factory orders excluding transportation since a 2.6 percent gain in April last year.
There have been other signs of a continuing modest pickup in manufacturing activity.
On Monday, the National Association of Manufacturers said its February index of activity rose to 53.1 from 52 in January as production and new orders increased.
Shipments of manufactured goods, which reflect more immediate demand than orders, rose 1.1 percent in January after a 0.7 percent decline in December.
Orders for non-defence capital goods, a measure of business' expansion plans, rose 5.3 percent in January to $46.2 billion after being flat in December.
Primary metals orders gained 5.2 percent to $15.9 billion after a 4.4 percent rise in December.
Orders for electrical and electronic machinery shot up by 16.6 percent to $28.1 billion in January after a 13.8 percent decline in December.
Order backlogs rose 0.9 percent in January to $518.9 billion -- a fifth straight month for higher unfilled orders -- pointing to continued vigour for manufacturing businesses in coming months.
